title: Wendell and the Silence
premise: Rosalind Joubert, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost her sense of taste years ago and has built a career on elegant evasion, learns that her late mother's house — the one she fled at nineteen after an accusation she never spoke aloud — is being auctioned by her estranged brother Wendell. Returning to settle the estate, she discovers her mother's journals, which reveal that her mother knew everything all along and chose silence to protect the family's standing. As the auction date closes in, Rosalind must decide whether inherited silence is loyalty or complicity. In the end she speaks the truth aloud at the auction itself — not to stop the sale, but to stop the lie — and walks away from the house with her taste for life, if not food, slowly returning.
about_author: Ada Kavanagh is the pen name of a former food writer who spent a decade covering restaurant culture before turning to fiction. She lives in coastal Maine, where she is at work on a second novel about families and the things they agree not to say.

chapters.title: The Palate
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A glittering review dinner in Manhattan where Rosalind writes rapturous prose about flavors she cannot taste, then goes home to a silent apartment. A letter arrives: the Joubert house is up for auction, and her brother Wendell expects her there. Emotional beat: the hollowness beneath a polished life.

chapters.title: What the House Remembers
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She drives back to her hometown and walks the shuttered house, where every room returns a memory she has spent twenty years editing — especially the summer her cousin Daniel lived with them. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into recognition; the past is not past.

chapters.title: Wendell
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell, meticulous and brittle, prepares the estate sale with his lawyer, convinced that selling quickly and cleanly is mercy. He resents Rosalind's return and guards a secret of his own about that summer. Emotional beat: love expressed as control, grief as logistics.

chapters.title: The Journals
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Packing the study, she finds her mother's journals and reads entries proving her mother knew what Daniel did — and chose the family's reputation over her daughter's voice. Emotional beat: betrayal re-experienced decades late; the floor gives way.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. At the funeral reception flashback interwoven with present-day estate inventory, Rosalind and Wendell circle each other in conversation made entirely of subtext. Each almost names the thing; neither does. Emotional beat: the family art of near-speech performed one last time.

chapters.title: Daniel Comes Back
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Daniel, now prosperous and beloved in town, appears at a pre-auction open house with his wife, charming everyone. Cornered in the kitchen where it happened, he offers Rosalind a settlement check and a warning. Emotional beat: power showing its face; fear meeting fury.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The auctioneer appraises the house while Wendell confronts his own journal-adjacent guilt: he suspected too, and buried it to keep his inheritance intact. He finds Rosalind reading on the porch stairs and, for the first time, asks her directly what happened. Emotional beat: the crack before the break.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The night before the auction, Rosalind tells Wendell the whole truth in the kitchen, naming Daniel, their mother's knowledge, and Wendell's own willful blindness. Wendell breaks — rage, then ruin, then something like relief. Emotional beat: catharsis; twenty years of silence ending in one long breath.

chapters.title: Going Once
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Auction day: bidders fill the lawn, Daniel attends in triumph, and when the auctioneer calls for objections, Rosalind stands and speaks the truth publicly, plainly, without apology. The sale proceeds anyway. Emotional beat: climax — justice outside the law, costly and irreversible.

chapters.title: Salt
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Weeks later, Rosalind resigns her column, eats a simple tomato sandwich at a roadside stand, and tastes it — faintly, truly, for the first time in years. She writes Wendell a short honest letter and receives a reply. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; inheritance refused, self reclaimed.
